Banzai Bill Competition Robot

Designed and built a 10 lb robot to compete in a Super Mario themed competition against other robots.

Requirements/specs

The robot had to complete five different tasks:

  1. Activate System (Leave the starting position)
  2. Deliver Mario (Raise a Mario figure to the top of a model castle)
  3. Defeat Koopas (Knock down two Koopa figures placed on either side of the robot)
  4. Feed Lumas (Collect small items (coins and starbits) from a rotating platform and deliver them on a slide)
  5. Eject Lumas (Shoot star-shaped figures into rotating slots)
12″ × 18″ × 24″Dimensions
40 sRun time
3.5 ft in 3.5 sTraverse speed
< 10 lbsWeight

Design exploration

Click a chart to enlarge it.

Challenges and design choices

Activation. Had a mousetrap system for activation initially, however, once the robot hit the center platform it would bounce back due to the acceleration from the mousetraps. We added a ratchet to eliminate this issue but the ratchet wore out easily so we just switched to using motors with a flange.

Eject Lumas subsystem: The blue is the Stabilize the Reactor subsystem. Once the limit switch is pressed by the rotating walls from the reactor, the motor stops moving and a pneumatic piston activates and shoots a Luma into one slot then retracts, allowing for another Luma to fall from the Luma tube. The piston doesn’t activate again until the limit switch is pressed by the next wall.

Deliver Mario subsystem: A motor begins to pull a string attached to a cascading lift. As the string is pulled, the lift extends over the base and towards a standing tower.

Feed Lumas subsystem: Has a collector that separates the coins and starbits by height and has them falling into cups.
Defeat Koopas: The two extending arms are a part of the Topple Koopas subsystem. Each arm has a cup attached to the front and after 25 seconds on the track, a solenoid triggers the mousetraps, revolving the arms to the side of the robot, hitting the Koopas, and placing the cups over the respective zones for the coins and starbits.

  • Pneumatics
  • Mechatronics
  • Arduino IDE

Work with Georgia Tech Experimental Rocketry

2024-2025 rocket: modular rocket holders

As part of GTXR’s 2024-2025 rocket, I designed and 3D-printed modular rocket holders to support a two-stage launch vehicle during ground operations. I iterated through multiple prototypes to optimize strength, weight, and stability within the constraints of a Bambu X1E 3D printer. The first iteration broke during our mock integration when a force perpendicular to the supports was being applied to the booster. I used a stronger infill density and printed the infill pattern so that it’s parallel to the direction of the force being applied on it. This worked a lot better and the supports lasted. I used PLA. These final holders were field-tested and successfully used during our launch in Mojave, California.

2025-2026 rocket: camera mount

As a part of GTXR’s 2025-2026 rocket, I designed a mount for a RunCam Thumb Pro camera for our two-stage solid-propellant rocket. The camera sits inside the nosecone near our avionics bay.

  • 3D printing
  • Iterative prototyping
  • SolidWorks
  • Classical mechanics

The Botanical Rickshaw: decorative houseplant holder

The Botanical Rickshaw is a scaled-down model of an auto rickshaw designed to function both as a decorative display piece and a houseplant holder. The roof features a built-in opening that securely accommodates a planter, transforming the rickshaw into a playful yet functional object.

Inspired by the cultural significance of auto rickshaws in India, the design draws from their instantly recognizable and iconic form. These vehicles are not only practical but also integral to daily life and the public transportation system. In this reinterpretation, the planter symbolizes the passengers typically found inside a rickshaw, blending cultural reference with natural elements.

Goal: design and 3D-print a decorative household item that provides a functional use as well.

Requirements

  • Project should have some sort of moving component
  • Minimum dimension that the printer can print is 0.1 mm

NestQuick: campus scooter charging station

Goal

design a product that would improve the quality of life of students around georgia tech's campus

NestQuick is a solar-powered vehicle charging station designed to reduce scooter and skateboard clutter on campus. Inspired by a tree, it features modular compartments for up to eight vehicles, a dome canopy for energy collection, and lights that show slot availability. Compact, sustainable, and visually appealing, NestQuick organizes vehicles while enhancing campus spaces.

This project was a group project that involved sketching, modeling, and pitching the product.

Requirements

  1. Product should include 10+ components
  2. Should have at least one moving part
  3. Should not cause a hindrance to students walking around campus
  4. Should be easy and intuitive for students
  5. Should blend in with the campus environment

Design targets

8Vehicle slots
10+Components
1+Moving part
SolarEnergy collection

Parts

  • Claw — Attachment that holds scooters; ferritic stainless steel (8)
  • Claw attachment — Attachment that locks the scooters; ferritic stainless steel (8)
  • Buzzcard scanner — ABS (8)
  • Cushioning under tree — Rubber (8)

Actuator Dynamometer for Lunar Rover

This project was a part of my work with Starpath, where I contributed to the design of a lunar mining vehicle. Most of the information relating to the project is confidential so the explanation given is limited.

Requirements

  1. The dynamometer should be able to test actuators experiencing a maximum load of 500 Nm
  2. The dynamometer should be able to test actuators under temperature conditions ranging from -70 C to 150 C

Test parameters

500 NmMaximum load
-70 to 150 CTarget temperature range
2Actuators
CSVRecorded test data

Due to budget and time constraints, the thermal subsystem of the dynamometer had to be put aside for the moment. The dynamometer I built recorded the outside temperature, recorded each motor's speed, efficiency, and the torque experienced. The efficiency of the motors were measured at two points: at the input of the actuator, at the output of the actuator.

The dynamometer consists of two actuators. One acts as the load actuator and the other acts as the test actuator. The load actuator provides a load speed while the test actuators hold a certain torque. I programmed a guided user interface that allows users to input load speed and torque values. This commands the ODrive PROs and their respective motor/actuator. Once the torque sensor experiences some torque, these values are read by the gain amplifier and then displayed on the GUI. The calculated efficiency values along with the thermocouple readings are displayed as well. All relevant values are saved as a CSV file and stored in the PI.

This process can be repeated for different sets of actuators. The goal is to determine the amount of current/power needed for each actuator along with verifying their overall performances.

Components

  • ODrive controller (2x)
  • K-Type Thermocouples (4x)
  • K-Type Thermocouple Amplifier - AD8495 Breakout board
  • ODrive dual shaft motors (2x)
  • ADS1115 Gain Amplifier
  • Rotary Torque Sensor
  • Actuator mounts (3x)
  • Torque Sensor mount (1x)
  • Power supply (x3)
  • Display for GUI
  • Motor mounts for testing
  • Breadboard (x2)
  • Breadboard mount
  • Raspberry PI
